name: The Outside Inn
subtitle: The outdoors, brought indoors, and asked to behave.
description:
The door is a door and behind the door is weather.

Not a conservatory. Not a courtyard with a roof off. Weather — thirty feet of it, going up, with a sky at the top that is doing something the sky outside is not doing. Tonight the outside sky is violet going crimson, as ever, and the Inn's sky is holding a clean cold noon with three-quarters of a moon in it, unbothered, like a man reading in a room where an argument is happening.

Beneath it: trees. Actual ones, rooted in actual ground that goes down further than the building's footprint permits. A stream comes out of the east wall, runs the length of the lounge, and goes into the west wall, and nobody has ever asked where from or where to. Over by the stair there is rain falling on one armchair and not on the one beside it, and both chairs are occupied, and neither occupant has mentioned it.
revisit:
The indoor sky has moved on to a dusk it is not entitled to at this hour, and the stream is running the way it ran on Tuesday rather than the way it ran last night, and there is a front due through the lounge at about ten.

Barney is behind the bar being robust at somebody. Bud is at the foot of the stair with one hand on the brass rail of a trolley that has not gone anywhere in eleven years and the grip is white at the knuckle. Somewhere near the water a narrow man in a good coat raises a hand to you, and so does the other one, and it is the wrong one, and neither of them minds.

lucid.2: There is a sound under the water-noise that the water-noise was chosen to cover.
lucid.3: The rain falls on the one chair because the chair beside it is not in the same paragraph.
lucid.4: The indoor sky is not a sky. It is a stage direction that ran long and had to be given somewhere to be.

ambient: A guest walks in from the street, shakes real rain off a coat, and steps under thirty feet of indoor weather without breaking stride or looking up, and hangs the coat where it will dry.
Dee Stroii passes through the lounge and simultaneously does not, and waves at himself from the stair, and the version by the water waves back with the other hand.
The stream carries a page of newsprint out of the east wall, turns it over twice on the good stretch, and takes it out through the west. Nobody reaches for it. It is not the first one this evening.

The front comes through at the far end of the lounge, four minutes early, and Barney's voice does the thing it does on the word 'sky' — warmer, slower, pitched at somebody small — and comes back to normal on the other side of it.
Bud tells a guest that the ceiling is a light well. The guest had not asked about the ceiling.

objects.name: the indoor sky
objects.description:
It starts about thirty feet up and it does not stop there.

That is the part that takes some standing under. There is depth in it — real depth, the kind the eye reads as distance rather than as a painted ceiling — and the moon in it tonight is three-quarters full and slightly the wrong way round for the season, and around the moon there are stars in arrangements that are almost, and are not quite, the arrangements you know.

The building is two storeys. You have walked past it four times in daylight and counted the windows.

Barney will tell you, at the smallest provocation and often at none, that the sky was here when he took the lease. He says it in exactly the tone a man uses to say that the boiler was here when he took the lease — mild, faintly proprietorial, and entirely without any sense that the two statements belong in different categories.
objects.repeat: The moon has not moved and the stars have, which is the wrong way round and has been the wrong way round every night you have looked, and the moon is at the same declination it was at on your first evening in this building.
objects.monocle: Through the gold there is no sky. There is a ceiling at nine feet, plaster, water-stained, with a light fitting in it that has been painted over. The thirty feet of night is being *described* into the gap between your eye and the plaster, and it is a good description, and in the top left of it there is a small mark like a proofing tick where somebody has read it back and been satisfied.

passive.text: The building is two storeys. You have walked past it four hundred times. There is no elevation here that can hold thirty feet of anything, and the room above this one is let, and somebody sleeps in it.

Watch the guests rather than the sky. Nobody looks up. In a room with a private night in the ceiling, not one person has looked up, and that is not incuriosity — that is a rule everybody has been taught and nobody was told.

clue.title: A private night indoors
clue.text: The Outside Inn contains thirty feet of independent sky in a two-storey building whose upper room is let and slept in. No guest ever looks up.

clue.title: A proofing tick
clue.text: Under the monocle the indoor sky is nine feet of water-stained plaster with a description laid over it — and in the top left, a small mark like a proofing tick, where somebody read it back and was satisfied.

check.prompt: There is thirty feet of sky in a two-storey building and a stream that leaves lower than it enters. Stand still in the middle of the lounge and let the place tell you what it is instead of asking it.
check.success:
It has weather in it.

Not the idea of weather, not a painted approximation of it — pressure, which the ears register before anything else does, and a front coming through with a leading edge you could put a hand up to, and a temperature drop that arrives here four minutes before it arrives outside.

Four minutes. Consistently. You have checked it twice against the door.

This sky is running ahead of the real one. It is not a copy of the weather over Silvora Reefs, and it is not a coincidence of pressure systems in a room with a stream in it. It is a draft of it.
check.failure:
Thirty feet of it, with a moon in it that is the wrong way round for the season, indoors, over a lounge with a stream running through it.

And the bellhop somewhere behind you saying BUT it's a light well — with the fervour of a man holding something up, at a volume calibrated to reach you and not the guests, and with a hand that has not left the brass rail of a trolley that is not going anywhere.

clue.title: A draft of the weather
clue.text: The Outside Inn's indoor sky carries weather four minutes before it reaches the real one. It is not a copy. It is a draft.

objects.name: the guest register
objects.description:
Open on the desk, because Barney keeps it open, because Barney holds that a closed book is an unfriendly object and has said so more than once to people who did not ask.

Name, arrival, room, and a column headed CAME BY. That last is the Inn's local peculiarity and Barney is quietly proud of it: guests write down which street they walked in from, and have done since he took the lease.

Harbour Road. Mountain Avenue. Harbour Road. Mountain Avenue. Wick Street. Harbour Road. Harbour Road. Mountain Avenue.

Nobody has ever queried it.

Mountain Avenue is on the far side of Silvora Reefs and it is uphill the whole way. Harbour Road is down at the water. They do not meet, they do not run parallel, and there is a parish between them — and both of them arrive at this door, and every single guest recorded in this book describes the walk as direct and none of them has ever recorded a turning.
objects.repeat: Four new arrivals since Tuesday. Two Harbour Road, one Mausoleum Hill, one with the CAME BY column filled in as 'the usual way', in a hand that is not Barney's and not any guest's.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the CAME BY column has a second entry under each first, in fainter ink, and every one of the second entries says the same thing: FROM WHERE THEY WERE LAST NEEDED.

passive.text: Check the arrival times against the streets. Two guests, four minutes apart, from opposite ends of the town, both direct, both on foot. One of those is a lie and neither of them is lying.
The column is headed CAME BY and not CAME FROM. Barney chose that wording, or somebody chose it for him, and 'came by' is what you say about a thing that arrived rather than a person who travelled.

clue.title: Every road arrives here
clue.text: The Inn's register records guests arriving directly from streets on opposite sides of town, minutes apart, on foot. Nobody has ever queried the column.

clue.title: From where they were last needed
clue.text: Under the monocle every register entry carries a second line in fainter ink: FROM WHERE THEY WERE LAST NEEDED.

check.prompt: A guest register, and you have read about guest registers — the trade has conventions, and conventions are how you catch a book that is being kept for a second purpose. Read the columns rather than the names.
check.success:
Registers are kept for the licensing and the licensing wants three things: arrival, origin, and duration. This one has all three and every origin is a place inside this parish.

Nobody has ever arrived at the Outside Inn from outside. In eleven years of a book kept for the express purpose of recording arrivals from elsewhere, there is no elsewhere in it.
check.failure: Names, dates, a column of origins in a careful hand. There is a shape to the way the book is kept that you have read about and cannot currently produce, and the innkeeper refills something at your elbow while you fail to produce it.

clue.title: Nobody arrives from outside
clue.text: Eleven years of the Outside Inn's guest register, and every recorded origin is somewhere inside the parish. There is no elsewhere in the book.

objects.name: the two armchairs
objects.description:
Side by side at the foot of the stair, eighteen inches apart. A matching pair, same upholstery, same wear on the same arm, the way two chairs wear when they have been sat in by the same two people for years.

It is raining on the left one.

It has been raining on the left one for as long as you have been in this room, and going by the state of the upholstery, for a great deal longer than that. The rain arrives out of the indoor sky in a column about a yard across — a defined column, with an edge to it you could put a hand through — lands on the occupant, runs off the occupant, and soaks away into a floor that is somehow keeping up with the volume.

The man in the left chair is reading a book. He is wet through to the collar and the pages he is turning are dry.

The woman in the right chair is knitting, in the dry, eighteen inches away. She has not looked over once. Neither of them has remarked on it, and neither of them is going to, and the ease between them is the most ordinary thing in the building.
objects.repeat: Still raining on the left. He has finished the book and started it again, and she has not once looked over at the eighteen inches of weather between them, and the two of them are entirely comfortable.

lucid.3: The eighteen inches between the chairs is not eighteen inches. It is a paragraph break.

objects.monocle:
Through the gold the two chairs are not in the same place.

They are in the same *sentence* — adjacent, separated by a comma, with nothing between them at all — and that is a different kind of adjacency and it explains the eighteen inches better than any amount of plumbing would.

One of them is being rained on because the clause says so. The other is not being rained on because its clause does not mention rain. Neither clause has been revised, and the man in the wet one has been reading in it for years, and the woman beside him has never once suggested that anything be changed.

check.prompt: Ask the woman in the dry chair whether her companion is getting wet. Do it kindly, and do it in a way that lets her not answer, because she has clearly been not-answering it for some time.
check.success:
"He likes it," she says, without stopping the needles.

And then, after four more stitches, in a completely different voice — flatter, and much older, and addressed to the knitting rather than to you:

"He's been in the wet one since March. I sat in it first, and it was dry, and then he sat down and it started, and I moved. That's all it is, love. It's not the chair. It's the one of us who's in it."

She does not elaborate. The needles go on. The man turns another dry page in the rain.
check.failure: "He likes it," she says, and the needles do not stop, and there is no second answer coming. After a while it becomes clear that there was never going to be a second answer and that standing here waiting for one is a thing you are doing to yourself.

clue.title: It's not the chair
clue.text: The woman in the dry armchair sat in the wet one first, when it was dry. It began raining when he sat down. Her verdict: it is not the chair, it is the one of you who is in it.

objects.name: the stream
objects.description:
It comes out of the east wall at ankle height, through an opening that has been finished with proper stonework — coursed, pointed, with a dressed sill — as though somebody had planned for a river at the design stage and hired a mason to receive it politely.

It runs the length of the lounge over a bed of rounded stones, drops about four feet into a pool by the bar with a noise the room has clearly been built around, and leaves through the west wall.

It is very cold and completely clear and there are small pale weeds in it, moving.

And it runs slightly uphill for the middle third of its course. Not steeply, and not obviously — just enough that a man who has watched water his whole life would stand at the rail for some time, faintly bothered, before he could say what it was that the room was doing to him.
objects.repeat: Running the other way tonight, and uphill for the middle third, and carrying rather more than it was — a page, a length of ribbon, something pale that turns over once and goes under before it can be identified.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the water is not water and is not pretending especially hard. It is a line of type running left to right along the floor of the lounge, in a face you have seen before, and where it drops four feet into the pool it is a paragraph break, and where it goes into the west wall it is the end of a page.

passive.text: Put a hand in it. It is cold in the way of a real stream and it pushes against the wrist in the way of a real stream, and it is doing that while going up, and the wrist has no opinion about which way is up.

It leaves through the west wall at a level below where it entered through the east, having gone up in the middle. That is a net loss of height accomplished with a gain in the middle, which water can do only if something is carrying it, and nothing is carrying it.

clue.title: Water running uphill in the middle third
clue.text: The Inn's stream runs slightly uphill for the middle third of its course, in both directions, and is otherwise entirely convincing water.

clue.title: A line of type along the floor
clue.text: Under the monocle the stream is a line of type running left to right, dropping four feet at a paragraph break and leaving through the west wall at the end of a page.

check.prompt: There is a stream running through the lounge and it goes out lower than it comes in, and nobody in this building has ever followed it. Get in it and follow it.
check.success:
The trick is to stop arguing with it. You go in to the shin and the current takes the leg and you let it, and it turns out to be the same negotiation as a wet deck in a swell, and the knees know it before the rest of you gets a vote.

Midstream the direction resolves: it is running toward the fireplace, and it has been running toward the fireplace for as long as there has been a fireplace, and nothing anywhere is filling it.
check.failure: You go in to the shin and the floor of it is not where the surface says it is. The leg goes further than the leg expected, the knee that has been going since the harbour makes its position known, and you come out of it wet to the waist with an audience being extremely tactful about it.

clue.title: It runs toward the fireplace
clue.text: The indoor stream at the Outside Inn runs uphill toward the fireplace and has no source feeding it.

objects.name: Bud's luggage trolley
objects.description:
Brass rail, brass wheels, brass everything, polished well past the point where polishing is doing any good and into the point where it is doing something else — a man's hands on the same rail, in the same two places, for years.

There are four bags on it. There have been four bags on it every single time you have been in this building.

They are not the same four bags. The tartan one was a leather valise in the spring and a hard case in the autumn and is a hatbox tonight. But there are four, always four, arranged with the big one at the bottom and the soft one on top, and the arrangement is correct, and it is the arrangement a man makes when he is about to move a trolley.

The trolley never goes anywhere.

Bud stands beside it all day with one hand on the rail, white at the knuckle, in the attitude of a man holding a horse for somebody who has said they are coming right back.
objects.repeat: Four bags. One of them is now a hatbox, and it was a valise on Tuesday, and Bud's hand has not left the brass rail in the whole of that time as far as anybody in this building can attest.
objects.monocle:
Through the gold there are no bags.

There is no trolley. There is no brass rail, no wheels, no hatbox and no valise.

There is Bud Onkuhdonk, standing in the middle of a lounge with one hand out at waist height, holding nothing, very hard, with the knuckles white — for a long time, on his feet, every day, in a building he believes he is helping to keep up.

And he is not wrong about that. That is the part the gold does not soften.

passive.text: He is not lazy and he is not idle. Look at the hand on the rail: the knuckles are pale. He is holding on to it. This is a man who has found one object in this building that will hold still and has decided to make a career of it.

clue.title: He is holding nothing, very hard
clue.text: Under the monocle there is no trolley and there are no bags. There is Bud, standing in the lounge with one hand out at waist height, gripping nothing, for a long time.

check.prompt: Bud has been holding that luggage trolley all evening and every evening before this one. Take the weight off him for a minute — properly, both hands, so he has to let go.
check.success:
He hands it over with enormous reluctance and you take the weight, and the weight is wrong.

There are no bags on it. There have never been bags on it. It weighs what a loaded trolley weighs and the load is not on it, and Bud watches you find that out with an expression of profound and specific relief at not being the only one.
check.failure:
He does not let go.

He says BUT it's no trouble, three times, with escalating politeness and no escalation whatever in the grip — and his knuckles do something on the third repetition that ends the offer considerably more clearly than a refusal would have.

He is not being rude. He is being, as far as he is concerned, extremely helpful, and he is going to go on being extremely helpful about this particular thing for as long as anybody stands near it.

clue.title: Loaded with nothing
clue.text: Bud's luggage trolley carries the weight of a full load and has nothing on it. He is relieved that somebody else has felt it.

objects.name: the fact of the weather
objects.description:
Thirty feet of lounge with a front coming through it at around ten. A stream that runs the correct way along the good stretch and the wrong way at the turn, which Barney says is the gradient. A ceiling that Bud Onkuhdonk would like it noted, at length, and without being asked, is a ceiling.

The weather is good weather. That is the thing that takes a while to arrive at: it is not merely present, it is *well done* — the front comes through at a believable pace, the light changes before the rain does, and there is a particular smell about four minutes beforehand that no one who had not stood outside in their life could have thought to include.

And Barney explains all of it in the voice he does not know he uses. It is warmer than his usual voice and slower and pitched slightly high, the way a man talks to somebody small who has asked what the noise is, and it arrives every single time on the word 'sky'.
objects.repeat: The front comes through again, on schedule, well made. Barney's voice changes again on the word 'sky' and comes back on the other side of it, and he has no idea it does this, and everyone who works here has stopped hearing it.
objects.monocle:
Through the gold the weather is a description running on a loop.

It is a good description. That is the part that stays with you: it is genuinely, carefully good — the light changing before the rain does, the smell four minutes ahead of the front, the way the far end goes soft first.

And it has been polished. Long after it worked, by somebody who kept coming back to it, adding a clause here and taking one out there, for years, in a room with no window, for the benefit of people who would never look up.

passive.text: The register he slips into is not for the guests. It is the voice used to tell a frightened person that the noise outside is only weather.

clue.title: Always weather, never architecture
clue.text: Barney explains the Outside Inn exclusively in terms of weather, in a register pitched at somebody small, and never once in terms of the building.

check.prompt: Stop asking how the Inn works; the answer is plumbing and everybody here has one. Ask what the Inn is a *picture* of.
check.success:
The Outside Inn. Read it as a phrase rather than a name and it stops being a joke about a sign.

It is a place for being outdoors, indoors. Weather without exposure, a stream without a journey, a sky with a lid on it — every good thing about being out, delivered into a room that can be locked, at a temperature somebody else is managing.

Nobody builds that for a traveller. A traveller can go outside. That is built, at considerable expense and with a great deal of care about the details, for somebody who cannot — and the whole parish comes here to drink under it and nobody has ever once asked who it was for.
check.failure: It rains indoors and there is a stream in the lounge and a bellhop who would rather you did not look up. The building resists being read as anything but the building, which after a fortnight in this town is almost restful.

clue.title: Built for somebody who cannot go outside
clue.text: The Outside Inn is the outdoors delivered into a lockable room — weather without exposure, sky with a lid. Nobody builds that for a traveller. It was built, carefully, for somebody who cannot go out.

exits.mobius: back onto the harbour road and the light that is nearly red
exits.lishush_mush: two streets in, toward a smell of something soft and extraordinary
exits.giddyup: up and inland, to smoke and a building older than the town
